page: Amazon Web Services d2.2xlarge is a storage-optimized virtual machine running on the Xen hypervisor, engineered primarily for dense local storage capacity. The hardware configuration includes 8 vCPUs across 4 physical cores of an Intel Xeon E5-2676 v3 processor operating at 2.4 GHz, paired with 61.0 GB of memory (7.62 GB per vCPU) and a 30 MB L3 cache. It incorporates 12,288 GB of local hard disk drive (HDD) storage, providing substantial bundled local disk capacity without additional block storage volume attachment. Network throughput is provisioned with a 2 Gbps baseline.

Benchmark results reflect the legacy Haswell microarchitecture and spinning-disk focus of the platform. Single-core execution scores fall into lower performance percentiles, registering 740.69 in stress-ng and 874.0 in Geekbench. Multi-core compute performance yields 4,142.49 on stress-ng and 3,265.0 on Geekbench, both placing in the bottom quartile. Memory bandwidth reaches 39.96 GB/sec on uncached large-block reads and 18.26 GB/sec on writes. Furthermore, static web serving throughput measures 5.44 GB/sec, while in-memory operations like Redis SET reach 2.47 million operations per second.

From an infrastructure cost perspective, the instance prioritizes raw local storage volume per virtual machine over high-density compute efficiency. The primary trade-off is diminished CPU clock speeds and low single-thread compute capabilities compared to modern NVMe-based or compute-optimized alternatives. It is best deployed for workloads requiring extensive local sequential storage capacity, including Hadoop/HDFS nodes, distributed log processing clusters, data warehousing staging nodes, and large-scale sequential data pipelines.

The architecture features 12,288 GB of integrated local hard disk drive storage, tailored for applications prioritizing massive bundled disk capacity over compute density. Standardized performance benchmarks reveal legacy architectural constraints, with Geekbench single-core scores of 874.0 and multi-core scores of 3,265.0 placing the system in lower percentiles.
